name: Cimetidine
lead: Cimetidine (brand name Tagamet) is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist that reduces stomach acid, used mainly for ulcers and heartburn. [1][2] It also has weak antiandrogenic activity, which is why it has occasionally been tried for acne and excess hair growth (hirsutism) in women. [2]

Wikipedia states that this antiandrogenic effect is too weak to help much with acne, hirsutism or hyperandrogenism in women, and that these uses are not recommended. [2] No clinical studies of cimetidine for appearance conditions are summarised in the sources used here.
infobox: Smith, Kline & French; marketed UK 1976, US 1977 [2]
Prescription in the UK and Australia; prescription and over-the-counter in the US [2]

paras: The labelled uses are duodenal and gastric ulcers, gastroesophageal reflux disease, pathological hypersecretory conditions and heartburn. [2][1] Dermatological uses such as warts, chronic urticaria and mastocytosis are off-label. [1]

Because cimetidine binds the androgen receptor very poorly and shows antiandrogenic effects mainly at high doses, it has been proposed for androgen-related skin and hair complaints in women. [2] Wikipedia describes the effect as insufficient for acne or hirsutism. [2] For common warts, early reports were favourable but double-blind trials found it no better than placebo. [2][1]

Side effects are usually mild and temporary and include diarrhea, rash, dizziness and fatigue. [2] Because of its hormonal effects, gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction are rare, with gynecomastia reported in roughly 0.1-0.2% of men on long-term treatment and more often at high doses. [2] The drug broadly inhibits cytochrome P450 enzymes and so interacts with many medications, including warfarin, theophylline and phenytoin. [2][1]

Cimetidine competitively blocks histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells. [1] Besides this, it weakly antagonises the androgen receptor and inhibits estradiol 2-hydroxylation, which can raise estrogen levels. [2] Oral bioavailability is 60-70% and elimination half-life is about 2 hours. [2]

Cimetidine was developed at Smith, Kline & French by a team including James W. Black and C. Robin Ganellin, following the earlier compounds burimamide and metiamide. [2][1] It reached the UK market in 1976 and the US in 1977 and became the first drug to exceed $1 billion in annual sales. [2]

No studies found for cimetidine in acne or hirsutism in the sources reviewed. Trials in warts, a related dermatological use, have given mixed results, with open-label reports of clearance and double-blind trials showing no advantage over placebo. [2][1]

timeline.event: Cimetidine synthesised at Smith, Kline & French. [1]
Marketed in the UK as Tagamet. [2]

card.summary: An acid-reducing H2 blocker with weak antiandrogen action that has been floated for acne and hirsutism; references describe the effect as too weak to matter.
card.note: Inhibits many liver enzymes and interacts with other drugs; rare gynecomastia.

quick.overview:
Cimetidine is an over-the-counter and prescription acid reducer. It has a weak antiandrogenic effect, so some have tried it for acne or excess hair in women.

Wikipedia reports that the effect is too weak to help those conditions and that such use is not recommended. No acne or hirsutism trials appear in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: It blocks histamine H2 receptors in the stomach lining, and at high doses weakly blocks the androgen receptor and affects estrogen metabolism.
quick.risks: Usually mild side effects such as diarrhea, rash, dizziness and fatigue; rare gynecomastia or sexual dysfunction, mainly at high doses. It inhibits liver enzymes and interacts with many drugs including warfarin and theophylline.
